topic: Cracking the Code: Information Theory and Entropy in Wordle
target_audience: University students (CS/Math background) or curious tech enthusiasts

sections.title: The Intuition: Why some guesses are 'better'
sections.content: Introduce the goal of Wordle as a search problem. Explain that a 'good' guess isn't just about matching letters, but about narrowing down the search space as quickly as possible.
sections.example: If you guess 'ARISE' and eliminate half the remaining dictionary, you've gained more 'information' than if you guess 'XYLYL' and eliminate almost nothing.

sections.title: Defining Information: The 'Surprise' Factor
sections.content: Define information content (Self-Information) as the negative log probability: I(x) = -log2(P(x)). Explain that rare events provide more information than common ones.
sections.example: Visual: A scale showing an 'Improbable Event' (a coin landing on its edge) creating a large spike in information versus a 'Common Event' (a coin landing on heads) creating a small flat line.

sections.title: Calculating Entropy: The Expected Information Gain
sections.content: Introduce Shannon Entropy as the average information (uncertainty) of a guess: H(X) = Σ p(x) log2(1/p(x)). A guess with high entropy splits the remaining word list into equal-sized buckets.
sections.example: Visual: A 'Bucket Analogy'. The word 'CRANE' acts as a sorting machine, distributing 2,300 words into various colored buckets based on the green/yellow/gray pattern result.

sections.title: The Strategy: Maximizing Entropy
sections.content: Show how an algorithm chooses a word not by looking for the secret word, but by looking for the word that produces the most 'informative' distribution of outcomes.
sections.example: An 'AI Detective' bot (modeled as a robotic fox) calculates entropy for every possible guess, selecting the one that 'tames' the uncertainty of the dictionary the fastest.

sections.title: Wrap-up: From Wordle to Reality
sections.content: Summarize how Information Theory principles apply to fields beyond games, such as medical diagnostics, data compression, and signal processing.
sections.example: Just as a detective eliminates suspects in a mystery, medical diagnostic trees use entropy to determine which test reduces the 'uncertainty' of a patient's condition most efficiently.
